Coral reefs are built by colonies of small marine animals called polyps,
which secrete calcium carbonate skeletons over many generations.

Reef-building corals rely on a symbiotic relationship with microscopic algae
called zooxanthellae. The algae live inside coral tissue and provide most of
the coral's energy through photosynthesis.

When ocean water becomes too warm, corals expel their zooxanthellae in a
stress response known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it
loses its main energy source and is more vulnerable to disease and mortality
if warm conditions persist.
